sections.h2: Who sends the Newark property tax bill?
sections.html:
The City of Newark Department of Finance bills and collects the tax. Essex County enters the picture only when an owner challenges an assessment. Inside Finance, the Assessments unit decides which real estate is taxable, keeps a tax map of every parcel and records changes in ownership and mortgages. Revenue Collections mails the bills, accepts payment and enforces collection when a bill goes unpaid.

To find out what a Newark property owes, call customer service Monday through Friday, 9 am to 4 pm, except holidays. The tax lines are 973-733-3791, 973-733-3792, 973-733-3962, 973-733-8098 and 973-733-3978. The city's Payment Center also takes tax payments online by credit card, debit card or electronic check. A seller who plans to list should call before the first showing, so the balance is known well before a contract is signed.

Newark bills in four installments, on the same quarterly dates that apply to every New Jersey town. Late amounts pick up interest, and a large delinquency adds a year-end penalty on top.

Newark installment dates and the late charges state law allows
InstallmentDue dateInterest ceiling on a late amount
FirstFebruary 1Up to 8 percent on the first $1,500, up to 18 percent above that
SecondMay 1Same ceiling
ThirdAugust 1Same ceiling
FourthNovember 1Same ceiling

A penalty of up to 6 percent can be added for delinquencies above $10,000 when the fiscal year closes.

Newark applies a partial payment to the oldest quarter still open. Say an owner has three quarters outstanding and mails a check in September. The money goes against the first quarter's principal and interest, and the later quarters stay open. For that reason the payoff on a closing statement can run higher than a quick tally of the latest bill suggests.

sections.h2: What happens to a Newark house when taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
The city sells a tax lien certificate on the property. Newark runs a standard tax sale for prior years' taxes and charges that are still owing, and an accelerated tax sale for current-year charges that remain due after the statutory date of November 10. State law, N.J.S.A. 54:5-19, covers taxes left over from the prior year.

  • The buyer of the certificate holds a lien and does not take title at the auction.
  • A town holder can sue to foreclose six months after the sale, and a private holder can sue after two years.
  • Before final judgment, an owner can demand in writing that the property go to a sheriff's sale so any equity is protected.
  • Redemption stays open until the Superior Court enters a judgment that bars it.

A separate New Jersey tax sale guide on this site covers redemption costs and the equity demand in more detail.

sections.h2: How to appeal your Newark assessment
sections.html:
Appeals go to the Essex County Board of Taxation on Form A-1, filed with the comparable sales form that goes with it. The petition must be filed and received by April 1, or by May 1 when the municipality has done a revaluation or reassessment. If the property is assessed above $1,000,000, the owner may file directly with the State Tax Court instead.

The burden sits with the owner, who has to show the assessed value is unreasonable against a market value standard. An assessment counts as excessive or discriminatory only if it fails both the true market value standard and the common level range, which is plus or minus 15 percent of the district's average ratio.

  • A county board judgment can be appealed to the Tax Court of New Jersey within 45 days.
  • An added or omitted assessment, which arises when a property is changed after October 1, is appealed on Form AA-1.
  • An added assessment above $750,000 in total may go directly to the Tax Court.

Newark is the county seat of Essex County and the largest city in the state, with an estimated 323,808 residents in July 2025 on 24.14 square miles of land. Owners occupy only 24.4 percent of homes. The middle value of an owned home is $373,700, median gross rent is $1,392, and the city counts 113,384 households with a median income of $52,060.

Since most households rent, a seller often deals with tenants already living in the building, and a buyer will want to see the leases. The city has five wards. Heavy industrial land near the airport and seaport sits mostly in the East and South wards, while homes cluster in the North, Central and West wards.

Transit helps a listing here. Newark Penn Station carries PATH, NJ Transit and Amtrak trains, and the Newark Light Rail links it to Broad Street Station. In 2020, 40.3 percent of Newark households had no car, so a short walk to a station is a real selling point for many buyers.

Ask Revenue Collections for a written statement covering every unpaid quarter, interest and any tax sale certificate, dated to the closing day. Whoever handles the closing pays that balance out of the seller's proceeds, which clears the lien for the buyer.

  • List every open quarter, including prior-year balances, since those can already be in a tax sale.
  • Check whether a certificate was sold and recorded, and find out who holds it.
  • If an assessment appeal is pending, tell your closing attorney so the filing is handled at closing.
  • Plan for the seller-paid realty transfer fee on the deed.

sections.h2: What should you line up before closing?
sections.html:
Start with the payoff. Once Finance gives you the written statement, hand it to the attorney or title company so they can wire the exact amount, interest included, on closing day. If a certificate exists, the holder discharges the lien after being paid, and the buyer receives clear title.

Next, gather your paperwork. Bring the latest tax bill, any notice from the county board if you filed an appeal, and the names of anyone who holds a mortgage on the house. If tenants live there, have the leases ready too.

A cash sale as-is skips repairs, showings and a buyer's lender appraisal, but it does not skip any of the tax steps above. The balance still comes out of the proceeds, and the lien still has to be cleared before the deed changes hands. Settling the number early is what keeps the closing date from slipping.

faqs.q: Who do I call to find out what I owe on a Newark house?
faqs.a: Call Newark's Finance customer service on a weekday between 9 am and 4 pm at 973-733-3791, one of five tax lines. Ask for the amount through your closing date.

faqs.q: By what date must a Newark assessment petition arrive?
faqs.a: The deadline is April 1, or May 1 if a revaluation or reassessment was done. File Form A-1 with the Essex County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the Tax Court.

faqs.q: What interest does Newark charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: Interest can reach 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent on the balance above that, under state law. A penalty of up to 6 percent can follow when the delinquency is over $10,000 at year end.

faqs.q: Does paying part of my bill stop a tax sale?
faqs.a: A partial payment is credited to the oldest quarter first, which cuts that quarter's principal and interest but leaves later quarters open. Newark can still sell a certificate for prior years' taxes that remain unpaid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Newark house that has a tax sale certificate on it?
faqs.a: Yes. The certificate amount and its interest come out of the sale price at closing, and the holder then discharges the lien. Get the payoff from the tax collector in writing so the title company can wire the exact amount.
